posts.content_md:
I am not familiar with QinetiQ's work.

> QinetiQ's Active Tiling system is a CGH modulator that requires conversion of an analog pixel array distribution into a binary distribution, with minimum degradation in the replayed image.

Would this not create harmonic noise seen in multiple orders?

posts.topic_title: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.author: Glenn
posts.post_subject: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.content_md:
> **Colin Kaminski:** I am not familiar with QinetiQ's work.QinetiQ's Active Tiling system is a CGH modulator that requires conversion of an analog pixel array distribution into a binary distribution, with minimum degradation in the replayed image.Would this not create harmonic noise seen in multiple orders?

Quinti-Q is a British defense contractor. Their Active Tiling system can create a screeen that easily supports 25M + pixels. It does this very simply. You have the following things:

1. An EASLM. 

2. OSLM

3. Lens array (array of little convex lenses--5 x 5)

4. Shutter array.

The idea is simple enough. Render on the EASLM (which is 5M x 5M LCD) a part of the holographic diffraction pattern. Just one part out of 25 parts, to be exact. Then, use the shutter to render the next diffraction pattern on each successive parts of the OASLM, for an image total of 5 x 5 diffraction patterns.

Since each diffration pattern is from a 5M x 5M LCD, you get a screen resolution of 25M by 25M pixels.

Here's your illustration of one of quinti-Q's modules:

[http://www.freepatentsonline.com/6927748-0-large.jpg](http://www.freepatentsonline.com/6927748-0-large.jpg)

> Dr Nasser Peyghambarian, chair of photonics and lasers at the university's Optical Sciences department, told CNN that scientists have broken a barrier by making the first updatable three-dimensional displays with memory.

This researcher actually got his chemicals from a laser scanner, as I recall. Here's your patent reference for his display:

[http://www.freepatentsonline.com/6221535.html](http://www.freepatentsonline.com/6221535.html)

The display reads with a red line and writes with a green line (or is it the other way around? Nonetheless, it's in the patent). The display itself is charged with 4Kvolts on either side.

posts.topic_title: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.author: Ed Wesly
posts.post_subject: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.content_md:
I just grabbed this thread, but it just is infuriating that once again TV is perverting holography! During the election results last night, there were two instances on CNN claiming that Will.I.Am was a holographic projection, and another I heard as local radio shock jock DJ Steve Dahl was mocking them for presenting some woman as a holographic projection. (He knows what they are, as I had sent him some holograms many years ago, being a loyal fan.)

I forget the woman's name, but she was describing the apparatus as 35 High Def video cameras surrounding her (where did they get that idea from, the LaserSmith's Holographic Moment rig?) and they talk to the monitors so you can see her all the way around, so she is the latest in a long line of holograms beginning with Princess Leia.

The latter is the only point that I can agree with! If I had the time, I'd sent CNN an angry blast-o-gram!

posts.topic_title: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.author: favalora
posts.post_subject: Another false promise of holograhic TV
posts.content_md:
Likewise, C|Net had an article about the holographic projection, as well. The journalist was very receptive to a note I wrote asking her to at least put quotation marks around the word holographic, which she did, and also was careful to edit the story to include a definition of hologram. Prior to that, a long list of argumentative comments had appeared under the story, which is here: [http://news.cnet.com/8301-11386_3-10082 ... icksArea.0](http://news.cnet.com/8301-11386_3-10082802-76.html?tag=newsEditorsPicksArea.0).

The best I can tell, it is of course multi-camera CG technology from Vizrt and SportVu.

Ed, over the last 10 years or so, computer scientists have gotten pretty good at software that takes multiple camera views as input and provides nearly arbitrary "what it looks like from somewhere else" output, like the Virtualized Reality (superbowl) work of [CMU's Prof. Kanade.](http://www.ri.cmu.edu/people/kanade_takeo.html) More recent stuff is from the really cool domain of light field rendering, like the ability to "shoot now, focus at home" but now I digress. (See ["Fourier Slice Photography"](http://www-graphics.stanford.edu/papers/fourierphoto/) at Stanford.) I apologize if you are already familiar with this stuff.

-g
